title: Listen!
speaker: Pastor Steve Brinegar

outline.title: The Command to Listen
subpoints: Listening is an active, not passive, engagement

outline.title: Being Swift to Hear
subpoints: Moving closer to understand the speaker

outline.title: Being Slow to Speak
subpoints: Avoiding interruption of the speaker's train of thought
Resisting the culture of soundbites and quick responses

outline.title: Being Slow to Wrath
subpoints: Anger destroys the ability to reason

outline.title: Application to the Word of God
subpoints: The command applies to receiving Scripture
God brings us forth by the word of truth
Receiving the implanted word with meekness

summary:
In this sermon, Pastor Steve Brinegar explores James 1:16-21, focusing specifically on the tripartite command in verse 19: to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath. He illustrates the necessity of active listening through the analogy of a fire captain who relies on trained intuition to detect danger, emphasizing that spiritual and communicative mastery requires deliberate practice and engagement. The sermon argues that listening is not a passive act but requires physical and mental effort, such as taking notes and positioning oneself to fully understand the speaker.

The message further addresses the cultural tendency toward rapid, fragmented communication, urging believers to resist the urge to interrupt or respond immediately. By remaining silent, individuals preserve the speaker's train of thought and allow for deeper understanding. Additionally, the sermon highlights the destructive nature of anger in communication, noting that wrath eliminates the capacity for reason and compromise, thereby hindering the exchange of ideas.

Ultimately, the sermon applies these principles to the reception of God's Word. It posits that the same discipline required for human interaction is essential for spiritual growth. Believers are called to receive the implanted word with meekness, recognizing that every good gift comes from the Father of lights. This active, patient, and humble approach to listening is presented as vital for being transformed by the truth.
